title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
titleZh: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
author: jaz
relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: watch nowNvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO, effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries.The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk." President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard."Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.Shares of Nvidia closed up 31% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6."I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNvidia stock chart.Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said. Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations. Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy." He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.""On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote. Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX, Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected."Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.Read more Nvidia newsHuang reinstatement reignites voter angst over tech's outsized powerJensen Huang's Nvidia return highlights U.S.-China AI talent raceNvidia whiplash tests Kevin Warsh's push to read market signals: LiesmanAI debt worries grow as Nvidia rebound masks Big Tech spending squeezeJensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession planTrump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in WashingtonAG Blanche, FBI's Patel dodge questions about Huang investigationCongress blasts Nvidia bringing Jensen Huang backJensen Huang to face Congress the same day as Nvidia GTCFor weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Nvidia's board formed an independent committee and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The board said Monday that "the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion" and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it.""The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia's board chair, Harvey Jones, said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."Even with Huang back at the helm, Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny over its chip sales in Southeast Asia and China. Lawmakers have been preparing for investigations into how Huang's affair with the alleged spy may have damaged U.S. AI dominance, influenced his positions on export controls, and impacted his close relationships with Trump and his Cabinet. Huang has been one of the loudest voices opposing strict export controls on advanced chips."The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a statement Monday. Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, is scheduled to appear before the panels on Dec. 2. Those dates were set before Huang's return, and John Fisher, who represents Huang, did not comment on whether there are any changes in his plans to testify.Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Monday that Huang will publicly testify on Dec. 3 as the sole witness during a hearing titled, "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls.""Americans deserve answers about what NVIDIA and the Trump administration knew, when they knew it, and whether sufficient steps were taken to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., a member of the Banking Committee, wrote in a post on X on Monday.WATCH: The rise, reinvention and uncertain future of Nvidia without Jensen Huangwatch now

comments.author: icyfox
comments.textRawHtml:
Some takes (and from talking to nvidia people):

- Delaware precedent in Caremark has a very high bar for culpability of boards in matters like this. So I suspect the combination of DoJ saying they won't prosecute combined with this standard will successfully remove their individual liability.

- I'm surprised this decision was completely unanimous at the board level, considering how they quickly forced him out. Full 180 in under two weeks.

- The news media is really confusing selling chips to Megaspeed then hosting them in Malaysia (giving chinese companies access - afaik still legal under the old export regime) and Megaspeed smuggling these physical chips for hosting in Chinese data centers. Former was legal and second was not.

- I would not be surprised if a pardon was mentioned at some point. Will be watching how state AGs end up getting involved. CA has already subpoenaed Nvidia for this.

- There was a drum circle at Nvidia from employees who were petitioning to get him back

Disclosure: I co-host a podcast that talks about this. More discussion if anyone is interested: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t8nLiELIhwA

children.author: etempleton
children.textRawHtml:
The reporting around this was pretty sloppy / showed a lack of understanding.

Most news reports would have you believe that this all happened yesterday when in fact it happened years ago. They also seemed to immediately believe that Jensen Huang was proven complicit in chip smuggling to China, which, as far as I am aware of, there is no proof of or really any insinuation of from legitimate sources. And then they would raise concerns about circular financing, which I agree is longer term a potential issue, but everyone jumped straight to Enron levels of financial manipulation, which I find a farfetched.

children.author: hn_throwaway_99
children.textRawHtml:
All of what you wrote feels like a bunch of strawmen designed to minimize Huang's significant misconduct:

> Most news reports would have you believe that this all happened yesterday

I literally don't know what you're talking about given that there were a ton of news reports that highlighted the US government was aware of Huang's affair in the early part of this year. A big part of this story was the US govt was aware of the affair for a long time and Trump himself was notified back in May.

> They also seemed to immediately believe that Jensen Huang was proven complicit in chip smuggling to China, which, as far as I am aware of, there is no proof of or really any insinuation of from legitimate sources.

Again, perhaps some Twitter-type news sources said that, but the mainstream media sources never made that link.

What is so enraging about Huang being reinstated is it is yet another case of "in your face oligarchy" with "rules for thee, but not for me". His conduct (having an affair with one of Nvidia's biggest customers whose primary business was making Nvidia compute available to China, having an affair with a direct report, having an affair with someone else at the company, and now it's being reported by WSJ he admitted to additional affairs at the Sunday board meeting) would get you fired from any company I can think of. I saw a spot-on joke that the employee handbook at Nvidia has been revised to "do whatever the fuck you want as long as you make money". The only reason he was reinstated is due to pressure from Trump because he wanted the stock market to go up.

Here’s a Google or AI agent phrase you can use: “what crime is Jensen Huang suspected of committing as CEO of Nvidia?” See? Easy.

Please, before you make comments, at least try to see if there’s anything out there that might contradict your own narrative. Otherwise you just look like a god damned fool who I’d barely trust to make a sandwich, let alone engineer anything.

children.textRawHtml:
When you’re a board member of a company and plausible information comes to light that your CEO may have committed serious crimes on behalf of the company, you fire the CEO immediately to contain the damage from spreading to you and to the existence of the company. You’re not going to let yourself be on the hook for criminal conspiracy once you come to learn these things. And your attorneys will advise the same.

You people don’t know jack shit about how the real world works.

children.author: meowlamoon
children.textRawHtml:
> real world works.

This is how real world used to work.

I hate to say this, but Nvidia is an old company, went public in 90s, when the trend was 1 share has exactly 1 vote.

If you apply the new trend where founders got class B 20x super voting share, like in Meta, SpaceX or any new company, Jensen is not going to be removed by board in the first place.

He will have 43% of the voting power by taking 3% of the share, and he effectively controls the board w/ little outside help.

It is not board fires him, but that he might be able to fire the board. And this is the brave new real world.

children.author: otterley
children.textRawHtml:
Espionage and violation of U.S. trade sanctions are exclusively Federal law, not state law. The states can’t prosecute these offenses.

Also, you don’t prove anyone innocent. Everyone is presumed innocent until proven guilty. I don’t presume Jensen Huang or Nvidia is guilty; I’m saying that if they are, they are now immune from prosecution. The board was thus able to rehire him under these conditions.
